data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Nevus sebaceous (of Jadassohn)** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. Write a short note on nevus sebaceous (PYQ).**
- Congenital hamartoma of the pilosebaceous–apocrine unit and epidermis (organoid epidermal naevus) — postzygotic HRAS/KRAS mutations; scalp (commonest), face, neck; ~0.3% of newborns

**Q2. Describe the three stages (clinical and histological).**
- Infancy/childhood: smooth, slightly raised, yellow-orange, waxy, hairless (alopecic) oval/linear plaque on the scalp; histology — immature hair follicles, small sebaceous glands
- Puberty (hormonal): becomes verrucous, thicker, more yellow, pebbly/cobblestoned; histology — papillomatous epidermal hyperplasia, abundant mature sebaceous glands, ectopic apocrine glands, absent terminal hairs
- Adulthood: development of secondary adnexal neoplasms — trichoblastoma (commonest), syringocystadenoma papilliferum, sebaceoma, apocrine tumours; BCC (true BCC uncommon, ~1%), rarely SCC, adnexal carcinomas

**Q3. What is Schimmelpenning syndrome (linear nevus sebaceous syndrome)?**
- Extensive nevus sebaceous with CNS (seizures, intellectual disability, hemimegalencephaly), ocular (colobomas, lipodermoids), skeletal (hypophosphataemic rickets), cardiac and urogenital anomalies; part of epidermal naevus syndromes

**Q4. Differential diagnosis.**
- Aplasia cutis congenita (atrophic/membranous, not waxy), epidermal naevus, juvenile xanthogranuloma, mastocytoma, solitary trichoepithelioma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum, congenital triangular alopecia, juvenile xanthogranuloma

**Q5. Management.**
- Observation with periodic examination vs prophylactic full-thickness surgical excision (often before puberty for cosmetic reasons/alopecia, and because secondary tumours may arise) — decision individualised (malignancy risk lower than once thought)
- Biopsy any new nodule or ulcer; CO2 laser/PDT for those unsuitable for surgery (risk of recurrence)

**Q6. What is the genetic basis?**
- Post-zygotic HRAS (≈ 90%) or KRAS mutations — RAS mosaicism; same mutations in Schimmelpenning syndrome and phacomatosis pigmentokeratotica

**Q7. Which tumours develop in nevus sebaceous?**
- Mostly benign, after puberty: trichoblastoma (commonest — previously misdiagnosed as BCC), syringocystadenoma papilliferum (second commonest), sebaceoma, apocrine adenoma/hidrocystoma, tricholemmoma
- Malignant (rare <1–2%): BCC, SCC, sebaceous carcinoma, apocrine carcinoma, porocarcinoma — usually in adults

**Q8. Clinical appearance at birth vs puberty.**
- Birth/infancy: smooth, hairless, yellow-orange, waxy, slightly raised plaque on scalp (linear/oval) — alopecic; Puberty: verrucous, pebbly, thicker (sebaceous gland hyperplasia under androgen influence); adulthood: tumour development (nodules within)

**Q9. Timing of excision — current view?**
- Prophylactic excision in childhood is no longer mandatory as malignant change is rare; excise for cosmesis, symptoms, or new nodules/ulceration; observation with periodic examination is acceptable; if excising, before adolescence gives smaller scars under local anaesthesia

**Q10. Histopathology by stage in detail.**
- Infancy: immature hair follicles, small sebaceous glands, papillomatous epidermis
- Puberty: hyperplastic, mature sebaceous glands opening directly onto surface, papillomatosis, ectopic apocrine glands in deep dermis, absent mature hair follicles
- Adulthood: secondary neoplasms (trichoblastoma, syringocystadenoma papilliferum)

**Q11. What is syringocystadenoma papilliferum?**
- Benign adnexal (apocrine) tumour, often arising in nevus sebaceous of scalp — papule/ plaque with crust and moist surface; histology — cystic invaginations with papillary projections lined by double layer of cells, plasma cell-rich stroma

**Q12. Dermoscopy of nevus sebaceous.**
- Yellow-white globules ('aggregated yellow-white globules') without hair follicles, brown globules/ papillary structures in older lesions; new nodules with arborising vessels suggest secondary BCC/ trichoblastoma

**Q13. Differential diagnosis in detail.**
- Aplasia cutis congenita (membranous, scarring), epidermal naevus, juvenile xanthogranuloma, solitary mastocytoma, congenital triangular alopecia, syringocystadenoma papilliferum, seborrhoeic keratosis (adults)

**Q14. Extracutaneous features in Schimmelpenning syndrome.**
- CNS (seizures, intellectual disability, hemimegalencephaly, Dandy–Walker), eye (colobomas, epibulbar dermoids), skeletal (rickets — hypophosphataemic via FGF23, bone cysts), cardiac, urogenital — mosaic HRAS/KRAS mutations

**Q15. Define and classify genodermatoses (PYQ).**
- Inherited disorders with skin manifestations — by inheritance: AD (NF1, TSC, Darier, Hailey–Hailey, EBS), AR (XP, lamellar ichthyosis, PXE, oculocutaneous albinism), X-linked recessive (X-linked ichthyosis, Fabry, Wiskott–Aldrich), X-linked dominant (IP, Goltz, CHILD, Conradi), mitochondrial, mosaic (epidermal naevi, McCune–Albright, Proteus)
- By function: keratinisation (ichthyoses, PPK), adhesion (EB), pigmentation (albinism, piebaldism), DNA repair (XP, Bloom), connective tissue (EDS, PXE, cutis laxa), tumour syndromes (NF, TSC, Gorlin), vascular (HHT), ectodermal dysplasias, immunodeficiency

## Quick spotter facts
- Yellow-orange waxy hairless plaque on scalp of a newborn — nevus sebaceous
- Trichoblastoma is the commonest secondary tumour

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Organoid naevi). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
